title: Ultrasonic Distance Sensor (HC-SR04)
learning_objectives: Explain how an ultrasonic sensor measures distance
Calculate distance from echo time using the speed of sound
Wire an HC-SR04 to an Arduino
Write Arduino code to read distance
Identify common measurement errors and limitations
introduction: The HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor measures distance by emitting a sound pulse and timing its echo. It is one of the most common sensors in robotics, used for obstacle detection, distance measurement, and navigation.
real_world_application: Obstacle-avoiding robots, parking sensors, liquid level measurement, and distance monitoring all use ultrasonic sensing. The HC-SR04 is affordable and easy to interface with microcontrollers.

core_concepts.definition: Sound waves with frequency above human hearing (typically 40 kHz for the HC-SR04).
The time it takes for a sound pulse to travel to an object and back.
The reflected sound pulse detected by the sensor's receiver.
Approximately 343 m/s in air at 20°C. Used to convert time to distance.
Input pin that starts the measurement. Requires a 10 µs HIGH pulse.
Output pin that goes HIGH for the duration of the echo return time.

step_by_step_explanation: 1. Connect VCC to 5 V, GND to ground, Trig to a digital output pin, Echo to a digital input pin.
2. In code: set Trig LOW, wait 2 µs, set Trig HIGH for 10 µs, then set Trig LOW.
3. The sensor emits 8 ultrasonic pulses at 40 kHz.
4. The Echo pin goes HIGH when the pulse is emitted and LOW when the echo returns.
5. Measure the HIGH duration of the Echo pin using pulseIn().
7. The division by 58 accounts for round-trip time and speed of sound (343 m/s ˜ 1/29.1 µs per cm, times 2 for round trip ˜ 58).

important_formulas.name: Speed of sound
important_formulas.variables: v = speed of sound in air

wiring_instructions: VCC ? 5 V, GND ? GND, Trig ? digital pin 9, Echo ? digital pin 10. Keep the sensor away from motors to reduce vibration noise.
diagram_specification: Arduino Uno connected to HC-SR04: Trig to pin 9, Echo to pin 10, VCC to 5 V, GND to GND.

code_examples.explanation: A 10 µs trigger pulse starts the chirp. pulseIn() measures the echo duration. Division by 58 converts to centimeters.

line_by_line_code_explanation: pinMode(trigPin, OUTPUT) — Trig is an output (we trigger the sensor).
pinMode(echoPin, INPUT) — Echo is an input (sensor tells us the time).
digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW/HIGH) — sends the trigger pulse.
delayMicroseconds(2/10) — timing for the trigger pulse.
pulseIn(echoPin, HIGH) — measures how long Echo stays HIGH.
duration / 58 — converts microseconds to centimeters (round-trip accounted for).

interactive_experiment.description: Move a virtual object and watch the measured distance update.
interactive_experiment.expected_behavior: Measured distance matches object position. Below 2 cm or above 400 cm, readings become unreliable.

expected_observations: Distance reading increases as the object moves away.
Distance reading decreases as the object moves closer.
Below 2 cm, the sensor cannot measure (too close).
Above 400 cm, the echo may not return (out of range).
common_mistakes: Forgetting the 10 µs trigger pulse (sensor does not fire).
Using the wrong pin for Trig vs Echo.
Not waiting between measurements (echo from previous pulse may interfere).
Ignoring the minimum distance (2 cm) and maximum range (400 cm).
Mounting the sensor near motors (vibration causes noise).
troubleshooting_steps: No reading (0 or very large): check wiring, check trigger pulse timing.
Erratic readings: add a small delay between measurements, check for interference.
Always reading 0: Echo pin may not be connected or may be on a non-interrupt-capable pin (if using interrupts).
Readings too high: object may be beyond range or at an angle.
safety_notes: The HC-SR04 operates at 5 V. Ensure your microcontroller supports 5 V inputs.
Do not point the sensor at people's ears at close range (ultrasonic can be uncomfortable).
In simulation, readings are idealized; real sensors have noise and angular limitations.

knowledge_check.question: Why do we divide the echo time by two when computing distance?
options: Because the sound travels to the object and back
Because sound loses half its energy
knowledge_check.correct_answer: Because the sound travels to the object and back
knowledge_check.explanation: The measured time covers the trip out and the return, so the one-way distance is half.

knowledge_check.question: If pulseIn() returns 1160 µs, what is the distance in cm?

mini_challenge: Modify the code to stop a motor when an obstacle is within 20 cm. Add a serial print showing 'OBSTACLE' when detected.
extension_activity: Research how to use two ultrasonic sensors for wider coverage and how to average readings to reduce noise.
assumptions: Speed of sound = 343 m/s (at ~20°C, sea level).
No temperature or humidity effects on speed of sound.
Single object in the sensor's cone.
intended_learning_outcome: Learner can wire an HC-SR04, read distance in code, and explain the time-of-flight principle.
